title: Governance, security and privacy
summary: Catalogs and ownership, PII classification, access models and masking, and how to honour erasure and retention in immutable, time-travelling storage.

blocks.text: Governance answers: *what data do we have, who owns it, who may use it, and how do we prove it?* Without it, a lakehouse becomes a place where nobody can find the right table and nobody dares delete anything.

items: **Data catalog**: searchable inventory of datasets with descriptions, schemas, owners, tags, lineage and usage. Populated automatically from metadata (warehouse, Iceberg catalog, dbt, OpenLineage), enriched by people.
**Ownership**: every dataset has an owning team (not a person) responsible for quality, access decisions and changes. Ownership lives in metadata so tooling can route alerts and access requests.
**Stewardship**: domain teams define business terms and classifications; the platform team provides the tooling and enforcement.

blocks.text: Make ownership a required field at creation time (a dbt `meta.owner`, a table tag, a catalog property) and fail CI when it is missing. Retrofitting owners onto thousands of orphan tables is far harder.

You cannot protect what you have not found. Classification labels columns and datasets by sensitivity, for example *public*, *internal*, *confidential*, *restricted*, plus specific types such as `pii.email`, `pii.national_id`, `pci.card_number`, `phi.diagnosis`.

items: **Automatic discovery**: pattern and sample-based scanners propose classifications (email regex, IBAN checksum). Warehouses such as Snowflake offer built-in classification; check the current documentation for coverage.
**Human confirmation**: scanners produce false positives (a `notes` column) and misses (free text containing phone numbers).
**Propagation**: tags should follow lineage, so a column derived from `email` is also tagged.

blocks.text: 34.3 Access models: RBAC, ABAC and policies

head: Model
Decision based on
Strength
Weakness
rows: Simple, auditable, native in every warehouse
Role explosion: region x domain x sensitivity
Attributes of user, data and context (department, tag, purpose)
One policy covers many tables via tags
Harder to reason about and audit
Roles for coarse access, tag-based policies for sensitive columns and rows

blocks.text: In practice: RBAC grants access to schemas and tables; tag-based masking and row access policies handle the sensitive parts. Grant to roles, never to individuals, and follow least privilege.

blocks.title: Snowflake: dynamic masking and row access policies

items: **Dynamic masking** hides values at query time based on role; the stored data is unchanged.
**Static masking** writes a de-identified copy, for example for dev environments.
**Tokenization** replaces a value with a token; a secured vault maps tokens back. Deterministic tokens keep joins working without exposing the value.
**Pseudonymisation** under GDPR is still personal data if re-identification is possible; only true anonymisation takes data out of scope.

blocks.text: Policies in the warehouse do not protect the same data read directly from object storage. If Iceberg files are readable by Spark with a broad storage credential, masking in Snowflake is bypassed. Enforce access at the catalog (credential vending) or keep sensitive columns out of shared files (chapter 24).
34.4 The right to erasure in immutable storage

GDPR Article 17 gives people the right to have their personal data erased without undue delay. Modern platforms make this hard by design: files are immutable, tables keep history for time travel, and backups exist on purpose. A `DELETE` statement is only the first step.

blocks.title: Erasure is a pipeline, not a statement
blocks.text:
DELETE customer 42 (Iceberg, merge-on-read)
  snapshot S5: data file F1 + delete file D1 -> row hidden, still in F1
  rewrite_data_files (compaction)         -> F1' without row 42  (S6)
  expire_snapshots older than S6          -> S1..S5 gone; F1, D1 deleted
  remove_orphan_files                     -> leftovers of failed writes
Also: Snowflake time travel + fail-safe, backups, downstream copies

blocks.title: Iceberg with Spark SQL procedures

items: **Iceberg**: with merge-on-read the row stays in the old data file until rewritten; until snapshots expire, time travel can still read it. Compact, then expire snapshots (which deletes unreferenced files) within your erasure deadline.

**Snowflake**: deleted data remains reachable through Time Travel for the table's `DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS`, then enters Fail-safe (for permanent tables, a further 7 days, recoverable only by Snowflake support). Use short retention on PII tables and document the Fail-safe window in your erasure policy.
**Backups and copies**: either expire them within the deadline or apply erasure on restore through a suppression list.
**Downstream**: every derived table, extract and ML feature store must be covered; lineage tells you where.

blocks.text: **Crypto-shredding** is an alternative for hard-to-rewrite storage: encrypt each person's PII with a per-subject key, and erase by destroying the key. It works well for event logs and backups but adds key management complexity.

blocks.title: Erasure SLA in a lakehouse
blocks.text: A subscription company must complete erasure within 30 days. The data platform team runs a weekly job: collect requests, delete by `customer_id` across all tagged tables found through lineage, compact affected partitions, expire snapshots older than 7 days, and record evidence per request.
items: Iceberg PII tables keep 7 days of snapshots; non-PII tables keep 30.
Snowflake PII tables use a 1-day retention time.
Backups older than 30 days are deleted; restores re-apply the suppression list.

**Retention policy** per data class: for example raw clickstream 13 months, invoices 10 years (legal), support transcripts 2 years. Implement it as automated deletes by partition plus snapshot expiry.
**Purpose limitation**: data collected for billing should not silently feed marketing models; tags can record allowed purposes.
**Audit**: log who accessed what and when (warehouse access history, catalog audit logs, storage access logs). Keep audit logs immutable and retained longer than the data they describe.
**Evidence**: regulators ask *prove it*. Keep records of erasure runs, policy changes and access reviews.

blocks.text: Retention and time travel interact: a table with 90-day snapshot retention still holds data you "deleted" by the 30-day rule. Align snapshot expiry and time-travel windows with the retention policy.

blocks.title: Governance design for a health-tech lakehouse
blocks.text: A health-tech company stores patient events in Iceberg, read by Spark, Trino and Snowflake. Analysts need aggregate access, a small clinical team needs identified records, and patients can request erasure. Design classification, access model, masking or tokenization choices, and the erasure pipeline, including where each control is enforced.
hints: Which engine could bypass your policies?
How do you prove an erasure request was completed?

items: Governance needs a catalog, team ownership in metadata, and stewardship by domains.
Classify and tag PII, confirm scanner output, and propagate tags through lineage.
Combine RBAC for coarse access with tag-based masking and row access policies for sensitive data.
Erasure in immutable storage = delete + rewrite + snapshot expiry + file cleanup, plus time travel, fail-safe, backups and downstream copies.
Retention policies and audit evidence must align with time-travel and snapshot settings.

blocks.q: After a DELETE on an Iceberg table using merge-on-read, why can the row still be recovered?
options: The old data file and earlier snapshots still exist until compaction and snapshot expiry
The delete is applied only in the catalog
blocks.explain: The delete file hides the row, but the original data file is still referenced by older snapshots. Rewriting data files and expiring snapshots removes it physically.

blocks.q: Which statement about Snowflake Fail-safe is correct?
options: Fail-safe follows Time Travel for permanent tables and is recoverable only through Snowflake support
Fail-safe applies only to transient tables
Setting retention to 0 deletes Fail-safe data immediately
Users can query Fail-safe with AT(TIMESTAMP)
blocks.explain: Fail-safe is a further period after Time Travel for permanent tables, not user-queryable. Transient and temporary tables have no Fail-safe, and retention settings do not shorten it.

blocks.q: Why does a masking policy in Snowflake not fully protect an Iceberg table also read by Spark?
options: Spark reading files directly with storage credentials bypasses the warehouse policy
blocks.explain: Warehouse policies apply to queries through the warehouse. Direct file access needs catalog-level controls or keeping sensitive columns out of shared files.

blocks.q: What is the main appeal of crypto-shredding?
options: It makes data anonymous under GDPR without any keys
Erasure by destroying a per-subject key, without rewriting every file and backup
blocks.explain: Destroying the key makes the encrypted values unreadable everywhere, including backups. It does not replace access control and adds key-management work.
